title: KV hash-segmentation prefetch exploratory notes
content:
Overview and motivation:

This is an exploratory note capturing a set of small experiments and hypotheses around using a lightweight hash-based segmentation layer on top of the KV residency allocator to reduce eviction-induced reuse loss and to make prefetching decisions more targeted to memory-bank locality. The core observation: global LRU-style admission/eviction continues to cause cross-bank page thrashing when multi-tenant/seqlen-skew workloads interleave, which amplifies NVMe paging and per-host memory-bandwidth spikes.

Goal:
- Measure whether simple static hash segmentation (N segments where segment = key_hash % N) reduces long-tail reuse loss and paging events compared to baseline global policy.
- See if segment-aware prefetch (only prefetch within segment boundaries) reduces cross-bank reads and lowers NVMe read amplification.
- Gather lightweight telemetry signals we can expose in metrics (segmented-reuse-hit-rate, seg-eviction-rate, seg-prefetch-success).

Design notes / hypothesis:
- Hash segmentation aims to confine a request’s likely KV footprint into a smaller physical locality set. Because our allocator maps hot logical keys to pages that happen to share memory banks, segmenting by hash should increase intra-segment reuse and reduce eviction churn that crosses bank boundaries.
- We keep segment count small (4, 8, 16) to avoid pathological fragmentation. Very large N increases cold misses.
- When a request touches keys that map across segments we default to cross-segment logic (no enforcement) — the scheme is advisory, not hard partitioning.
- Prefetch policy: when a key is read and its segment is under a low-occupancy threshold, issue a small prefetch of adjacent keys within that segment (configurable stride 4–16). The idea is to prefetch within predicted locality without triggering cross-bank fanout.

Experiments run (short IDs referenced below):
- run-2024-06-14-A: baseline global LRU-ish allocator + current async prefetch (no segmentation).
- run-2024-06-15-B: static hash segmentation N=4, no prefetch; eviction threshold unchanged.
- run-2024-06-16-C: N=8 + segment-local prefetch (stride=8), prefetch budget 0.5% of req tokens.
- run-2024-06-18-D: N=16 + aggressive prefetch (stride=16), prefetch budget 2%.
- run-2024-06-20-E: N=8 + segmentation + adaptive prefetch throttle (prefetch inhibited when host bandwidth > 70%).

Workloads used:
- mixed-chat: multi-tenant chat traces, seqlen distribution heavy tail (median 64, 95th 1024). This is the main target.
- retriever-sim: synthetic high-embedding density access (many small keys per request).

Key telemetry captured:
- reuse_rate: fraction of key hits vs misses (sampled per-segment and global).
- eviction_rate: evictions per second, per-segment.
- paging_events: NVMe read count and bytes triggered by spillback.
- mem_bw_p95: 95th percentile host DRAM read BW.
- prefetch_success_rate: fraction of prefetches used before eviction.
- tail_latency_p99: request-level latency p99 (important to track regression).

Findings (high level):
- run-2024-06-15-B (N=4) reduced global eviction_rate by ~9% on mixed-chat compared to baseline; observed a modest +3% improvement in reuse_rate for top segments.
- NVMe paging_events dropped by ~7% for B vs baseline (same provisioning). Bank-local read amplification decreased slightly (measured via per-NUMA read counters).
- run-2024-06-16-C (N=8 + conservative prefetch) improved reuse_rate by ~12% vs baseline and reduced tail latency p99 by ~4% in mixed-chat. Prefetch_success_rate ~62% (meaning 62% of prefetched keys were used before eviction).
- run-2024-06-18-D (N=16 aggressive prefetch) saw diminishing returns: reuse_rate improved only +6% vs baseline but NVMe read amplification increased (more unnecessary prefetch reads), mem_bw_p95 increased ~11% and p99 latency regressed slightly under burst.
- run-2024-06-20-E (adaptive throttle) retained most benefits of C while avoiding BW spikes: mem_bw_p95 back down to baseline+1–2% and prefetch_success_rate improved to ~68%.

Observed micro-behaviors (profiling notes):
- Evictions became more correlated within segments (good) — we saw localized eviction cascades instead of global churn that touched many pages across banks.
- When tenant workloads had strong cross-key locality but keys hashed to different segments, segmentation hurt (because it prevented co-placement by locality). This is visible in retriever-sim: segmentation increased misses when the natural locality set didn’t align with hash clusters.
- Prefetch pacing matters: naive aggressive prefetch floods DMA engine and causes NVMe queueing -> read amplification. Adaptive throttle based on instantaneous DRAM BW and NVMe queue depth is effective.
- Metadata overhead is low: segment id per key is a single byte stored in our residency catalog; lookup latency negligible in hot path.

Quantitative table (approx, aggregated across 3 runs each):
- Baseline (A): reuse_rate 0.318, eviction_rate 62/s, nvme_reads 12.1MB/s, mem_bw_p95 67GB/s, p99 210ms
- B (N=4): reuse_rate 0.346, eviction_rate 56/s, nvme_reads 11.3MB/s, mem_bw_p95 64GB/s, p99 205ms
- C (N=8 + pref): reuse_rate 0.357, eviction_rate 51/s, nvme_reads 10.7MB/s, mem_bw_p95 63GB/s, p99 201ms
- D (N=16 aggressive): reuse_rate 0.339, eviction_rate 58/s, nvme_reads 14.9MB/s, mem_bw_p95 74GB/s, p99 224ms
- E (N=8 adaptive): reuse_rate 0.362, eviction_rate 49/s, nvme_reads 10.9MB/s, mem_bw_p95 65GB/s, p99 198ms

Interpretation and tradeoffs:
- Small number of segments (4–8) plus conservative segment-local prefetch seems to be the sweet spot for mixed-chat like traces. It reduces eviction churn and paging without large bandwidth cost.
- Aggressive prefetch (larger stride, higher budget) is easy to mis-tune and increases read amplification; this can hurt tail latency under bursts.
- Hash segmentation does not play well when application-level locality is orthogonal to hash; for retriever-style workloads, an access-pattern-aware grouping (hot-set fingerprinting) is better than static hash. Consider hybrid approach: prefer co-placement heuristics if sampling indicates keys frequently co-accessed across segments.
- Adaptive throttle (based on instantaneous mem BW and NVMe queue depth) is essential when enabling prefetch in noisy multi-tenant environments.

Potential production rollout sketch (minimal-risk):
- Stage 1: enable segmentation N=8 as an advisory metadata field only (no prefetch), collect segment-level telemetry across canary fleet for 4 weeks.
- Stage 2: enable conservative segment-local prefetch (stride=8, budget=0.5%) behind feature flag + throttle tied to a mem_bw gauge and NVMe queue metric. Canary 2% traffic for 2 weeks.
- Stage 3: evaluate hybrid co-placement sampling to remap hot co-accessed keys into the same segment via background mover if beneficial.

Open questions / next experiments:
- Can we cheaply learn a per-tenant ideal segment mapping (adaptive small remap) without high metadata churn? (Idea: bloom filter sketches per tenant of frequent co-accesses.)
- How does segmentation interact with quantized model footprints where KV page sizes change? Need to test with 4-bit quantized model runs.
- Explore non-power-of-two segment mapping to avoid alignment with bank-interleaving patterns that currently exist in our allocator mapping (bank interleaving + mod N collisions cause skew).
- Investigate a per-segment admission bias (slightly favor admitting larger keys into underutilized segments) — might reduce cold misses for big-embedding workloads.

Action items (who/when):
- Diego: run longer 7-day canary for N=8 on mixed-chat small % fleet and dump segment-level telemetry (start 2024-06-28).
- Marcus: add mem_bw and nvme_qdepth signals to prefetch throttle hook (PR in linked_artifacts) and add a debug trace when throttle triggers (due 2024-07-02).
- Priya: prototype simple bloom-coaccess sketch per tenant and measure remap candidate precision on last-90d trace (due 2024-07-10).
- Ava: compile a short ops-runbook for rollback if prefetch causes NVMe queueing; include runbook thresholds (rollback if nvme_qdepth > 120ms for >5min).

Notes to self / random observations:
- For debugging, sample 0.1% of requests and capture full key lists + segment ids; this gives good signals to detect cross-segment hot access patterns without huge overhead.
- Flame graphs of eviction stack show that a few tenant patterns dominate eviction churn; adding per-tenant segment affinity might substantially reduce global churn.
- When we talk about "segmentation" internally, be explicit this is advisory (logical grouping) not hard reservation — we want flexibility to break out when cross-segment locality exists.

Appendix: short debugging checklist for experiments
- verify segment assignment distribution: `histogram(segment_id)` should be approx-uniform (if not, check hash function or mod bias).
- check per-segment residency skew: if certain segments always >2x occupancy, they may be attractors; consider rehash or remap.
- compute "co-access score" between keys: pairs seen in same request window / total — helps find candidate remaps.
- sample nvme latency tail while toggling prefetch to ensure prefetch does not amplify queueing.

Summary:
Hash-segmentation combined with conservative segment-local prefetch looks promising for mixed-chat workloads — it reduces eviction churn and paging with small CPU/metadata cost. The major caveat is workloads where logical locality is not aligned with hash segments; for those, a co-access aware remapping or different heuristic should be used. Next step is cautious canary telemetry collection + implement adaptive prefetch throttle production hooks.

End of notes.
